newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair hopes to push Northern Irish talks.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair hopes to push Northern Irish talks.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair will on Wednesday set out the proposals with which he hopes to spark life into stymied talks on the future of Northern Ireland.

The plan, which Blair drew up with outgoing Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, centres on an attempt to persuade the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to call a new cease-fire which would in turn allow its political arm Sinn Fein into the talks.
In fact, Blair's key recommendation is the adoption of "parallel decommissioning", a proposal made in January 1996 by George Mitchell, the former U.S. senator who now chairs the year-old peace talks.
The term means that the IRA -- and its rival Protestant guerrillas -- would give up their caches of arms in stages while the talks proceeded.
Blair's predecessor, John Major, was criticised for rejecting this element of Mitchell's proposals.
But Major, who was ousted in a May 1 election, was under severe pressure from the pro-British unionist and loyalist politicians from Northern Ireland who shored up his tiny parliamentary majority.
With Blair's landslide election win, the Protestant politicians who want Northern Ireland to remain under British rule have lost much of the sway they held over the peace process.
Nevertheless, most appeared philosophical about Blair's plan.

David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, Northern Ireland's main Protestant party, his deputy John Taylor and senior MP Ken Maginnis were the first of the Northern Ireland politicians to meet Blair on Tuesday morning to hear about the proposals.
When he emerged from Blair's Downing Street office, Trimble said parallel decommissioning was not his party's "first preference."
He added: "We indicated that we could go along... provided of course that that is what actually happened."
But hard-line Democratic Unionist Party leader Ian Paisley accused London and Dublin of having "given in to the IRA" and said his party might quit the all-party talks.
The proposal got a warm reception from John Hume, the leader of the nationalist SDLP who was instrumental in bringing about the IRA's now defunct cease-fire in 1994.

Asked after meeting Blair whether the peace process was on the verge of a breakthrough, Hume said: "I certainly hope that we are and I believe that given the tense atmosphere on our streets...it is the duty of everyone to do everything they can to reduce that tension."

The IRA abandoned its cease-fire in February 1996, blaming the British government's intransigence in refusing Sinn Fein entry to the talks until the guerrillas, who want an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, disarmed fully.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams pledged to study the Blair-Bruton proposal carefully once it was made available.
None of the Northern Irish politicians has yet seen the 12-page document.

It was expected to have been presented at peace talks on Tuesday, but Blair was forced to soothe feelings in Tuesday's talks with the Northern Irish party leaders after Bruton said in a television interview the proposals had been agreed.
Bruton, in New York with Blair on Monday for a United Nations environment summit, said the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in the multi-party talks.
But Blair backtracked, saying: "I think it's possible that we have the basis of a way forward. But of course this has got to be agreed with all the other parties."

Blair, who is now due to unveil the proposals in a statement to parliament on Wednesday, said all possible clarification had been provided to Sinn Fein, which now had to choose between the political path and violence.
The "troubles" in Northern Ireland is one of the world's longest-running guerrilla conflicts, claiming the lives of more than 3,200 people over the last 28 years.
